title: A Generational Gap
text: “Father, how does this compare for me, I wonder?”
“Motoyasu-kun, I don’t think there’s that much difference from my era…”
“Indeed, that does seem to be the case. It was in the form of operating in front of a personal computer.”
“Well, there’s not that much of a gap between Motoyasu-kun’s world and mine. Anyway, let’s ask the two of them. Motoyasu-kun, it seems like you already know a bit about Itsuki’s side.”
According to Father, he mentioned that the development history of the game had a rather unique story behind it.
“Oh? What kind of history was it?”

“…It costs nothing to tell, so I don’t mind sharing. Let’s skip the story details, though. It was a game where you finished Volume 1 by defeating Dragon King, and then dug into the conversion elements for the rest.”
That Dragon King in question apparently took the form of the dragon Takt was housing, I say. Since we’ve already saved the world—cleared it, so to speak—there’s no need to worry about it, indeed.
“In the end, that knowledge turned out to be a trap anyway.”

“Setting that issue aside for now, let’s talk about the circumstances behind Dimension Wave’s development. In a sense, it was a revolution that occurred in the gaming industry… though there’s also a strong possibility that the truth is that some mastermind trying to destroy the future set it up as a trap.”
“That ominous a story, huh?”
“Yes. First, there’s a game I need to mention. It wasn’t called Dimension Wave, but if this game hadn’t come out, Dimension Wave never would have seen the light of day.”
“Ah, yeah, that happens. The kind where, looking back, every game afterward turns out to be built on the foundation of that one game.”

“In terms of category, it’d be hack-and-slash. This one originated in my world about thirty years ago—a PC-exclusive adult doujin game whose demo alone, titled ‘Name Undecided,’ caused a massive sensation despite being a full 2TB in size.”
“Name Undecided… what a title. And more importantly, 2TB… for just the program files, that’s incredible.”
“Is it really that impressive?”
Ren tilted his head slightly at this.
“Well, Ren’s from the most sci-fi-advanced Japan among us, so 2TB might not seem like such a big deal to him.”
“This is where you really feel the generational gap.”
“…I see. I knew there were various differences even within the same ‘Japan,’ but so the gap starts around there, huh.”
“Yes, well, Kou isn’t quite on Ren-san’s level. Even with his extraordinary abilities.”

“Still, a world where a 2TB hard drive existed thirty years ago is impressive in its own right, Itsuki. If we were all from the same world, Itsuki would literally be calling me and Motoyasu-kun ‘old man’ or ‘grandpa.’”
By the way, apparently in Father’s world, 2TB is just a normal range for a hard drive in an average household PC, I say. Of course, there are hard drives with even greater capacity than that, indeed.
“Anyway, back to the game Itsuki knows about. Apparently some wealthy person bought it, rights and all, and then disappeared—something like that, according to what Itsuki said before.”

“Yes, it was sold for an extremely high price, bundled together with the distribution rights. Even at the demo stage, it had an incredibly high degree of freedom and was said to be terribly addictive.”
“That’s quite the story. Sounds like you could play that one forever.”
“I’ve actually seen a bit of it in videos online. It was tremendously popular—apparently the downloaded hard drives, even just for the demo, were being traded for huge sums of money.”
“Turning everything into money, huh… guess that’s just human nature. You’d think the original poster would’ve stepped in, but whoever actually made the thing is just too mysterious.”
“I can’t deny that. To this day, nobody knows who created it.”
“Wouldn’t be surprising if it turned out to be someone from another world entirely. Like, say, the true form of that princess the first me—the one Motoyasu-kun knows—ended up defeating.”
Indeed, that does seem plausible, I say. It must have been that much of an out-of-place artifact, even by Itsuki’s era’s standards.

“Even though it was just a demo, it got regular updates and eventually ballooned up to 10TB. Apparently they couldn’t keep up anymore, so they had to split it into different versions. There were almost no hard drives that could hold the final version, so people resorted to jury-rigging multiple drives together just to fit it all.”
“Whoa… 10TB… now that’s a proper monster of a file. Downloading that would take forever. If your connection was weak, you’d probably never even finish.”

Given the connection speeds of the time, even just downloading it would’ve been brutal, I say. Ren, not quite following the technical details, simply nodded along repeatedly as if to say “sure, whatever you say.” In his era, that kind of capacity was apparently nothing to write home about, indeed.
“Anyway, the game I was playing—Dimension Wave—was created by analyzing that ‘Name Undecided’ demo and imitating parts of it.”
“No telling where the enemy got involved in all this, but it really was a strange and roundabout path that led to that game existing.”
“Yeah… so, Ren-san, how did the VR games in your world come about?”
“Might as well start from Itsuki’s example. Apparently it originated from equipment and programs used to train soldiers during a war about fifty years back.”
“Ah… there’s a similar story in my world too—games originally being military computer tech repurposed for peaceful use. Guess major technological revolutions really do tend to come out of conflict.”
Indeed, that does seem to be the case, I say. Most great inventions are born out of strife.

“From there, research progressed until people’s consciousness could enter the internet. The first officially recognized dive game was Brave Star Online, but before that there was a deeply entrenched competitive game—one where you fought using a customized avatar. The avatars used across the internet these days are all just repurposed versions of that original system.”
“Not quite a game in the usual sense? Was Brave Star Online something you logged into using that same avatar?”
“No, in Brave Star Online you create a separate character of your own, apart from the avatar you use elsewhere online.”
“Sounds like there’s some kind of boundary unique to Ren-san’s world that I’m not quite getting.”
“Is it something like the pre-installed games that come with a computer right out of the box?”
The kind like Sol●taire or Mi●esweeper, I say. Something about that comparison makes me want to throw up, indeed!
“Ah… yeah, maybe it is kind of like that. It’s a game, sure, but more like… lame, or something in that vein.”

“I won’t deny that, but it’s deeply entrenched and massive in scale. The variety of competitive formats is huge too… honestly, it had more players than Brave Star Online, which felt like a proper different-world game through and through. Strong players were awarded crown-shaped accessories, and to get a copy of one, you had to have that person personally acknowledge your strength in a match.”

Depending on how much of a handicap your opponent granted you going into the match, the serial number of the accessory you’d win would be determined accordingly, or so Ren explained, I say. Apparently if you faced someone who was genuinely serious, the accessory you received would have incredibly elaborate ornamentation, indeed. And naturally, whoever held the original was a top-ranker, I say. They apparently had epithets too, like “Four Heavenly Kings” or “Champion,” indeed. Somehow that side of things sounds like a lot more fun.
“I guess if it’s a game that everyone who dives into the net starts out with, that makes sense. Kind of a ‘simplicity is best’ deal. So, does that connect to something?”

“Ah… when you move around within the net, you can freely alter your appearance, so besides a human form you can also take the shape of a robot, an animal, all kinds of things. Kids especially tend to prefer animal avatars, so…”
“Ah, I see—so Ren, having been diving into the net and playing since he was little, doesn’t feel much discomfort even in a form like Inault’s.”
“So the reasoning is that if you’ve already experienced it before, changing your appearance isn’t an issue—that makes sense. By the way, Ren-san, how good were you at that game, skill-wise?”
Ren suddenly fell silent, I say. I recognize this pattern, indeed!
“Ah, you got taken out by a headshot, didn’t you!”
“Shut up! Don’t lump me in with those monsters who could dodge through a hail of attacks like that!”
“Oh, so there really were monsters who could dodge that stuff. Well, every game’s got someone absurdly good at it.”

It seemed to have hit the mark dead-on, I say. Ren glared at Father with visible irritation for some reason, indeed. No, wait… he was actually glaring at the float shield Father had deployed just in case, indeed. I really don’t quite understand it, I say.
